blocks.text: 1. Gradient Calculation

blocks.alt: A loss produces a gradient showing the direction to reduce loss

blocks.text: Chain Rule, already shared with the traditional Machine Learning course, provides the mathematical tool for handling nested functions. Gradient Calculation applies that exact rule systematically across an entire computational graph, not just one isolated function.

This connects back to Computational Graph, the previous topic, whose explicit, node-by-node structure makes this systematic process genuinely possible, giving the chain rule a clear, complete map to actually apply itself across.
2. What a Gradient Actually Means

blocks.alt: A gradient points in the direction of steepest increase

blocks.text: This connects back to the weight and bias adjustment already covered in the Weights and Biases topic. A gradient tells exactly how much, and in which direction, the loss actually changes for a tiny nudge to one single specific weight.

This is precisely the information training needs to decide how to adjust every weight, increase it slightly, decrease it slightly, or leave it essentially unchanged, in order to gradually reduce the loss over the course of training.
3. A Brief Reminder of the Chain Rule

A brief, direct reminder of the Chain Rule itself is worth stating clearly here. For a chain of nested functions, one function's output feeding directly into the next, the overall derivative equals the product of each individual function's own derivative.

This exact mathematical fact, already covered in genuine depth in the traditional Machine Learning course, is the entire mathematical foundation everything else covered throughout this topic actually builds directly on top of.

blocks.text: 4. Local Gradients

blocks.alt: Each operation has its own local gradient

blocks.text: This connects back to each individual node in the computational graph, already covered in the previous topic. Every single node has its own simple, local gradient, its own individual derivative with respect to its own direct inputs.

A multiplication node's local gradient, for instance, is simply the other input's value, a genuinely straightforward calculation at the level of any single node, regardless of how complex the overall network actually is.
5. Chaining Through the Graph

blocks.alt: Local gradients multiply together into the full gradient

blocks.text: Starting from the loss node, at the very end of the computational graph already covered in the previous topic, gradient calculation multiplies local gradients together, working backward, node by node, all the way from the loss back toward the earliest weights.

Each weight's final, full gradient is the product of every local gradient along its specific path through the graph, directly applying the Chain Rule already reviewed earlier in this topic, one connected step at a time.
6. When a Weight Affects the Loss Through Multiple Paths

blocks.alt: A weight affecting the loss through path one and path two has its gradients summed

blocks.text: A genuinely important detail is that some weights affect the loss through more than one single path, directly connecting back to the fully connected structure already covered in the Layers topic, where every neuron connects to every neuron in the next layer.

In this case, the correct approach is to sum the gradients contributed by every single separate path a weight actually influences, ensuring the weight's final gradient correctly accounts for its full, total influence on the loss, not just one of several paths.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: Forgetting to sum gradients across multiple paths is a genuinely common source of subtly incorrect gradient calculations, especially in fully connected layers where this multi-path situation is actually the norm, not the exception.

blocks.text: 7. Numerical Versus Analytical Gradients

blocks.alt: A numerical gradient is approximate and slow while an analytical gradient is exact and fast

blocks.text: Two genuinely different ways exist to actually compute a gradient. The numerical approach nudges a weight slightly and measures the resulting change in the loss directly, genuinely simple to understand conceptually, but far too slow for any real, practically-sized network.

The analytical approach applies the Chain Rule directly, exactly as covered throughout this topic, considerably faster, and exactly what real Deep Learning frameworks actually use during genuine, practical training.

blocks.text: 8. Gradient Checking

blocks.alt: An analytical gradient gets compared to a numerical one, catching bugs

blocks.text: A genuinely practical use for the slower, numerical approach already covered in the previous section is verifying that an analytical gradient calculation is actually correct, comparing the two approaches' results directly against each other.

This is called gradient checking, a genuinely useful debugging technique covered in further practical depth in the Training Deep Networks module later in this course, catching a subtly incorrect analytical gradient calculation before it silently corrupts an entire training run.
9. A Preview of Vanishing and Exploding Gradients

This connects forward to the vanishing gradient problem, already introduced in the Sigmoid topic. Multiplying many small local gradients together across many layers, exactly the chaining process already covered throughout this topic, can shrink the final gradient toward zero.

Or, in the opposite case, it can grow the final gradient toward an enormous, unstable value instead, called the exploding gradient problem, both covered in far more practical depth in the Backpropagation topic immediately following this one.
10. Why This Understanding Matters Before Backpropagation

Understanding gradient calculation clearly matters directly before Backpropagation, the very next topic in this module, since backpropagation is genuinely just this exact process, made efficient and fully automatic across an entire network at once.

Understanding the underlying mathematics first, covered fully throughout this topic, makes the algorithm itself considerably easier to actually follow, rather than treating backpropagation as an unexplained, opaque procedure with no clear mathematical grounding.
11. Worked Example
The example below computes gradients by hand through a small computational graph, directly applying the chain rule covered throughout this topic.

code.content:
# Forward pass: x -> multiply by w -> add b -> relu -> loss
x, w, b = 2.0, 0.5, 0.1
y_true = 1.5

multiply_out = x * w          # 1.0
add_out = multiply_out + b    # 1.1
relu_out = max(0, add_out)    # 1.1
loss = 0.5 * (relu_out - y_true) ** 2  # squared error loss

print(f"Forward pass: multiply={multiply_out}, add={add_out}, relu={relu_out}, loss={loss:.4f}")

# Backward pass: applying the chain rule, node by node, exactly as covered in this topic
d_loss_d_relu = relu_out - y_true                    # derivative of the squared error loss
d_relu_d_add = 1.0 if add_out > 0 else 0.0           # local gradient of relu
d_add_d_multiply = 1.0                                # local gradient of addition
d_multiply_d_w = x                                    # local gradient of multiplication, w.r.t. w

d_loss_d_w = d_loss_d_relu * d_relu_d_add * d_add_d_multiply * d_multiply_d_w
print(f"\nGradient of loss with respect to w: {d_loss_d_w:.4f}")
print("Computed by chaining each node's local gradient together, exactly the process covered in this topic")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This example explicitly names each local gradient before multiplying them together, directly demonstrating the chaining process covered throughout this topic, the exact same mechanism backpropagation automates across an entire network.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Gradient Calculation applies the Chain Rule systematically across an entire computational graph.
A gradient tells exactly how much and in which direction the loss changes for a tiny weight nudge.
Every node has its own simple, local gradient, its own individual derivative with respect to its inputs.
Working backward from the loss, local gradients get multiplied together along each weight's specific path.
When a weight affects the loss through multiple paths, its gradients from each path must be summed.
The numerical approach is simple but slow; the analytical approach, using the chain rule, is fast and practical.
Gradient checking uses the slower numerical approach to verify an analytical gradient calculation is correct.
Multiplying many small local gradients together can cause vanishing or exploding gradients, covered further next.
Next up: Backpropagation, the efficient, automatic algorithm that performs exactly this process across a full network.
